scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originates within the Kuruba community of Karnataka as a form of worship for Lord Mailara Linga.
It is tied to the 'Deekshe' initiation, where men dedicate their lives to the deity and the Gorava sect.
The tradition involves the recitation of epics like those of Mailara Linga, Manteswami, and Mahadeshwara, which are central to the community's identity.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at festivals, local fairs, and private housewarming ceremonies known as 'Mane Seve' or 'Ogu Seve'.
It is a ritual of devotion meant to honor the deity and bless the homes of devotees.
The 'unruly' behavior in private settings represents a state of divine possession or total surrender.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: In public, 10-12 dancers stand in a straight line before moving into circles.
The senior Gorava leads with the flute and damaru.
Dancers use 'big eyes' and raised eyebrows to create a fearsome look.
Watch for Ogu Seve Eating, Scary Gaze.

Formation: Straight lines for 10-12 people, transitioning into circular paths.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instruments are the 'Damaru' (a small drum) and the 'Pillangovi' (flute).
Dancers also wear 'Gante' (jingles/anklets) that provide rhythmic percussion.
Listen for the Damaru (small drum), Pillangovi (flute), Gante (jingle/anklets).
A dense percussive layer of small drums and heavy metal anklets overlaid with high-pitched flute melodies and deep, repetitive vocal chanting of religious epics.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The most distinctive feature is the bear-skin headgear worn over a white 'Rumala' (turban).
Dancers wear a white or yellow 'Panche' (waist cloth) and a white 'Juba' (shirt).
They carry a 'Nagabetha' (wooden stick) and a 'Jolge' (bag).

scenes.title: The people
narration: The 'Guru' or head of the Gorava clan is the central figure who initiates new members.
The senior-most Gorava in a performance group acts as the conductor, initiating the music and movement.
While primarily a Karnataka tradition, the performance style varies between the 'unruly' private ritualistic form and the more disciplined, choreographed public folk form.
The tradition is passed through the 'Deekshe' initiation, a formal oath-taking ceremony where boys are accepted into the sect by the clan head in the presence of the deity.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Goravara Kunitha is a religious initiation rite; dancers are sworn devotees who have taken an oath (Deekshe). Outsiders should respect the 'Mane Seve' as a private religious service and avoid interfering with the ritual offerings or the bear-skin headgear which is considered sacred.
